source.version: No full text on file; the CHI 2026 version of record (doi 10.1145/3772318.3791329) returned HTTP 403 at dl.acm.org. Read instead: arXiv 2411.00168 v1 of 2024-10-31 (earlier title 'Creativity in the Age of AI: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Design Outputs and Designers' Creative Thinking', 18 pages), read in memory with pymupdf, plus the CHI 2026 abstract from Semantic Scholar. Page numbers below are arXiv v1 PDF pages. The CHI abstract reports the same 36 participants but adds ratings by online volunteers, which v1 lacks, so CHI statistics may differ from v1.
source.title_on_document: Creativity in the Age of AI: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Design Outputs and Designers' Creative Thinking

paper_design_summary: In a lab experiment with counterbalanced order, 36 participants each made social media advertisements in two 25-minute sessions: one with ChatGPT and DALL-E 2, one without AI. A random half did the AI session first. Five blind expert raters from the client organization scored the 105 eligible designs for usefulness, creativity, unconventionality (weirdness), brand alignment, and visual appeal. Participants also took the Alternative Uses Test and an anagram test after each session.

studies.label: Within-subjects lab experiment (social media ad design with and without GenAI)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of conditions (GenAI-supported session first or human-only session first); every participant did both conditions
assignment.quote: A randomly selected half of all participants were first assigned to design individually, with the second half assigned to design with GenAI.
assignment.locator: p. 7, Section 3.3 Procedures (also p. 2, Fig. 1 caption: 'randomly assigned to two groups ... counterbalanced order')
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 8, Section 3.4, second paragraph: protocol preregistered; the planned analysis by self-reported design skill was abandoned. No registration URL or identifier is printed. p. 8, Section 4, second paragraph distinguishes primary preregistered design-outcome analyses from exploratory subgroup analyses.

arms.name: GenAI-supported
arms.description: Designed with the ChatGPT web app (ChatGPT Plus, DALL-E 2 text-to-image); other tools allowed to fix AI text or clip images

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Designed individually with tools of the participant's choice, without AI

participants.exclusions: Five designs were excluded for non-compliance with study requirements, leaving 105 eligible designs (52 human-only, 53 GenAI-supported). No participant exclusion is reported, and the number of people represented in the design-outcome analysis after those exclusions is not separately stated (p. 8, Section 4).
participants.who: 36 participants recruited through professional and academic channels (Slack, Discord), email lists, and fliers on a large public US university campus; 94% under 30, 81% women, and 67% with some GenAI design experience (p. 6, Section 3.1). All participants completed both design sessions (p. 3, Introduction; p. 6, Section 3). The CHI title calls them novice designers. The preprint does not establish a student-only sample. The post-exclusion analyzed-person count is not separately reported; 105 is the number of eligible designs, not people (p. 8, Section 4).
participants.quote: We recruited 36 participants via professional and academic communication channels (Slack, Discord, etc.), email lists, and fliers posted on a large public university campus in the United States.
participants.locator: p. 3, Introduction (all participants completed both sessions); p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.1 (36 recruited, demographics); p. 8, Section 4 (five excluded designs and 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only, 53 GenAI-supported)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT web app (ChatGPT Plus accounts) with DALL-E 2 text-to-image model
ai_tool.how_used: Participants prompted ChatGPT to generate and modify advertisement images in a 25-minute session; other tools were allowed to correct AI-generated text or clip images (p. 6 Section 3.2; p. 7 Section 3.3).

task.description: Create one or two 1080 x 1080 pixel social media advertisements promoting a newly launched research group website; top-three designs earned a $40 bonus
task.duration: 25 minutes per design session; whole study about 90 minutes

outcomes.name: Expert-rated creativity of the design ('This design is creative', 7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five client-organization experts blind to condition each evaluated the entire eligible design set (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3). There were 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only and 53 GenAI-supported (p. 8, Section 4). Section 3.4 names Wilcoxon signed-rank tests but does not state how ratings were aggregated across reviewers or multiple designs per participant, or the test observation counts. The statistical analysis unit and denominator are unconfirmed, so unit and n_units are null. Reported design-rating SDs are not established as participant-level SDs.

contrasts.reported: GenAI-supported M = 3.909, SD = 1.389 vs human-only M = 3.457, SD = 1.359; Z = -3.318, p < .001 (Wilcoxon signed-rank); '13% more creative'

outcomes.name: Expert-rated unconventionality ('This design is weird', 7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five client-organization experts blind to condition each evaluated the entire eligible design set (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3). There were 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only and 53 GenAI-supported (p. 8, Section 4). Section 3.4 names Wilcoxon signed-rank tests but does not state how ratings were aggregated across reviewers or multiple designs per participant, or the test observation counts. The statistical analysis unit and denominator are unconfirmed, so unit and n_units are null. Reported design-rating SDs are not established as participant-level SDs.

contrasts.reported: GenAI-supported M = 4.262, SD = 1.328 vs human-only M = 3.457, SD = 1.250; Z = -5.958, p < .001 (Wilcoxon signed-rank); '23.3% more unconventional'

outcomes.name: Expert-rated usefulness ('In a social media ad campaign, how well will this ad perform?', 11-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Five client-organization experts blind to condition each evaluated the entire eligible design set (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3). There were 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only and 53 GenAI-supported (p. 8, Section 4). Section 3.4 names Wilcoxon signed-rank tests but does not state how ratings were aggregated across reviewers or multiple designs per participant, or the test observation counts. The statistical analysis unit and denominator are unconfirmed, so unit and n_units are null. Reported design-rating SDs are not established as participant-level SDs.

contrasts.reported: No difference: Z = -0.238, p = .812 (Wilcoxon signed-rank); arm means shown only in Fig. 3 (p-value 0.812). The same Z and p are printed on p. 8 for an unrelated test of self-reported design skill.

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Test (AUT) fluency after each design session
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Fluency is the total number of uses listed across the two objects (p. 6, Section 3.2). After each design session, participants completed the AUT in Qualtrics following a brief mood and self-efficacy survey, before the Anagram Test. Each AUT used two everyday objects, with two minutes per object; objects differed across sessions and were randomly assigned. One researcher coded fluency, flexibility, and originality using the counting method in reference [4] (p. 6, Section 3.2; p. 7, Section 3.3; p. 8, Section 3.4). This is an immediate post-session test of the participant, coded after_ai. Overall analyses and exploratory prior-GenAI-experience subgroup contrasts are kept separate. Analyzed-person counts for these contrasts are not separately printed.

contrasts.reported: Overall sample: Section 4.2 reports no significant condition difference in inherent divergent thinking (AUT). No facet-specific overall arm means, SDs, test statistic, exact p value, or analyzed-person count is printed.

Exploratory subgroup without prior GenAI design-tool experience: post-GenAI M = 14.333, SD = 4.384 vs post-human-only M = 12.500, SD = 4.573; Z = −2.112, p < .05 in the text. Figure 4 prints p = 0.035. The subgroup analyzed-person count is not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.2.1; p. 9, Fig. 4, Fluency-No AI Exp. panel

contrasts.reported: Exploratory subgroup with prior GenAI design-tool experience: no significant condition difference; Figure 4 prints p = 0.208. Arm means and 95% confidence intervals are plotted without exact value labels; arm means, SDs, test statistic, and analyzed-person count are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Fig. 4, Fluency-With AI Exp. panel and caption; p. 10, Section 4.2.1

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Test (AUT) flexibility after each design session
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Flexibility is the variety of idea categories within one participant’s AUT responses (p. 4, Section 2.1), not diversity across people. After each design session, participants completed the AUT in Qualtrics following a brief mood and self-efficacy survey, before the Anagram Test. Each AUT used two everyday objects, with two minutes per object; objects differed across sessions and were randomly assigned. One researcher coded fluency, flexibility, and originality using the counting method in reference [4] (p. 6, Section 3.2; p. 7, Section 3.3; p. 8, Section 3.4). This is an immediate post-session test of the participant, coded after_ai. Overall analyses and exploratory prior-GenAI-experience subgroup contrasts are kept separate. Analyzed-person counts for these contrasts are not separately printed.

contrasts.reported: Overall sample: Section 4.2 reports no significant condition difference in inherent divergent thinking (AUT). No facet-specific overall arm means, SDs, test statistic, exact p value, or analyzed-person count is printed.

Exploratory subgroup without prior GenAI design-tool experience: post-GenAI M = 12.250, SD = 3.562 vs post-human-only M = 10.167, SD = 3.131; Z = −2.203, p < .05 in the text. Figure 4 prints p = 0.028. The subgroup analyzed-person count is not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, Section 4.2.1; p. 9, Fig. 4, Flexibility-No AI Exp. panel

contrasts.reported: Exploratory subgroup with prior GenAI design-tool experience: no significant condition difference; Figure 4 prints p = 0.714. Arm means and 95% confidence intervals are plotted without exact value labels; arm means, SDs, test statistic, and analyzed-person count are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Fig. 4, Flexibility-With AI Exp. panel and caption; p. 10, Section 4.2.1

outcomes.name: Alternative Uses Test (AUT) originality after each design session
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality concerns the uniqueness or novelty of a participant’s ideas compared with other participants’ ideas (p. 4, Section 2.1). It is coded as novelty of the responses, not across-person diversity; the paper gives no further scoring formula. After each design session, participants completed the AUT in Qualtrics following a brief mood and self-efficacy survey, before the Anagram Test. Each AUT used two everyday objects, with two minutes per object; objects differed across sessions and were randomly assigned. One researcher coded fluency, flexibility, and originality using the counting method in reference [4] (p. 6, Section 3.2; p. 7, Section 3.3; p. 8, Section 3.4). This is an immediate post-session test of the participant, coded after_ai. Overall analyses and exploratory prior-GenAI-experience subgroup contrasts are kept separate. Analyzed-person counts for these contrasts are not separately printed.

contrasts.reported: Overall sample: Section 4.2 reports no significant condition difference in inherent divergent thinking (AUT). No facet-specific overall arm means, SDs, test statistic, exact p value, or analyzed-person count is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2; p. 4, Fig. 2 and Section 2.1; p. 8, Section 3.4

outcomes.name: Anagram Test convergent-thinking performance after each design session
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants rearranged prompt words into anagrams for three minutes; the number of completed words was their final score (p. 6, Section 3.2). This test followed the AUT after each design session in Qualtrics, using different prompt words in the second session (p. 7, Section 3.3). It is an immediate after_ai outcome. The source does not specify human versus automated scoring, and the codebook has no exact measure category for answer-count scoring, so measure is null. No contrast-specific analyzed-person count is printed.

contrasts.reported: Overall sample: no significant condition difference in convergent thinking (Anagram). Overall arm means, SDs, test statistic, exact p value, and analyzed-person count are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 4.2; p. 6, Section 3.2 (score definition); p. 7, Section 3.3 (timing)

outcomes.name: Expert-rated visual appeal (7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts rated the statement "This design is visually appealing" on a 7-point scale (p. 7, Section 3.2). Five client-organization experts blind to condition each evaluated the entire eligible design set (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3). There were 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only and 53 GenAI-supported (p. 8, Section 4). Section 3.4 names Wilcoxon signed-rank tests but does not state how ratings were aggregated across reviewers or multiple designs per participant, or the test observation counts. The statistical analysis unit and denominator are unconfirmed, so unit and n_units are null. Reported design-rating SDs are not established as participant-level SDs.

contrasts.reported: No significant condition difference: Z = −0.456, p = .649 (Wilcoxon signed-rank). Arm means, SDs, and test observation counts are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 3.4 (test); p. 7, Section 3.2 (measure)

outcomes.name: Expert-rated alignment with the client organization (7-point scale)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts rated how effectively the design represented the client organization on a 7-point scale (p. 7, Section 3.2). Coded as usefulness because it assesses appropriateness to the client brief. Five client-organization experts blind to condition each evaluated the entire eligible design set (pp. 7-8, Section 3.3). There were 105 eligible designs: 52 human-only and 53 GenAI-supported (p. 8, Section 4). Section 3.4 names Wilcoxon signed-rank tests but does not state how ratings were aggregated across reviewers or multiple designs per participant, or the test observation counts. The statistical analysis unit and denominator are unconfirmed, so unit and n_units are null. Reported design-rating SDs are not established as participant-level SDs.

contrasts.reported: No significant condition difference: Z = −1.213, p = .225 (Wilcoxon signed-rank). Arm means, SDs, and test observation counts are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 4.1; p. 8, Section 3.4 (test); p. 7, Section 3.2 (measure)

eligibility.reason: Randomized within-person crossover: the order of the GenAI and human-only sessions was assigned at random (p. 7, Section 3.3), and experts rated the resulting designs (pp. 7-8, Sections 3.2-3.3). Only 36 participants were recruited, and all completed both sessions (p. 3, Introduction; p. 6, Sections 3 and 3.1). The post-exclusion analyzed-person count is not separately stated, so n_analyzed is null. The study cannot reach the 50-person threshold even if all recruited people contributed eligible designs. The 105 eligible designs after five design exclusions are outputs, not people (p. 8, Section 4). It remains a small randomized experiment listed in the screening report and excluded from the core dataset; no context class applies.

one_line_finding: With 36 participants in a crossover lab experiment, experts rated GenAI-supported ad designs more creative (M = 3.909 vs 3.457, Z = -3.318, p < .001) and more unconventional (4.262 vs 3.457, Z = -5.958, p < .001) but not more useful (Z = -0.238, p = .812) (arXiv v1, pp. 8-9, Section 4.1, Fig. 3).
